en.title: Will it snow in the next 3 weeks? Atlas, Alps, Pyrenees, US-Canada and Andes from ECMWF, NOAA and NASA (24 November 2026)
en.description: A science-based snow outlook to mid-December 2026 for five mountain ranges: the 50-member ECMWF ensemble for days 1-15, NOAA GEFS for days 16-21, NASA MODIS for the snow on the ground today. Chance of more snow than the 1991-2020 normal: Atlas 4 %, Alps 10 %, Pyrenees 46 %, US-Canada West 88 %, Andes 12 %.
en.lede: Nobody can tell you today whether it will snow in Chamonix on 12 December. What science can do is something more honest: give the odds. We took the full 50-member ECMWF ensemble run of 24 November 00 UTC for the next 15 days, the NOAA GEFS ensemble for days 16 to 21, the NOAA forecasts of the big circulation patterns (NAO, AO, PNA, AAO) and NASA's MODIS snow maps of the last 8 days, and turned them into one number per mountain range: the chance that the next 15 days bring more snow than a normal late November and early December (1991-2020). The answer is very different from one range to the next. The western US and Canada lead with 88 %, the Pyrenees are a coin toss at 46 %, the Alps sit at 10 % despite a snowy week ahead, and the Atlas is almost certainly dry at 4 %.

sections.h: Three time scales, three kinds of forecast
p: A weather forecast does not lose its skill all at once. For the first 5 to 7 days the ensemble members mostly agree, and a snowfall total can be read almost like a deterministic number. Between day 8 and day 15 the members spread out and the useful information is the probability. Beyond two weeks, the sub-seasonal range, the day-to-day weather is no longer predictable, but slow drivers such as the North Atlantic Oscillation or the Madden-Julian Oscillation still tilt the odds for whole weeks (Vitart 2014; Vitart and Robertson 2018; Cassou 2008).

So we split the outlook in three windows: 24 to 30 November (days 1-7) and 1 to 8 December (days 8-15) from the ECMWF ensemble, then 9 to 14 December (days 16-21) from NOAA's GEFS, the only open ensemble that runs that far every day. For each window we compare with the same calendar days in the 1991-2020 climate record of ECMWF, on the same 0.25° grid, so a bias of the grid itself cancels out in the ratio.

Each ensemble member i gives a snowfall total S_i, in millimetres of water, summed over the window: S = Σ s_t. To turn water into fresh snow we use Δh = S · ρw / ρnew with a fresh-snow density ρnew of about 100 kg/m³, so 1 mm of water is about 1 cm of new snow. Judson and Doesken (2000) measured mean fresh-snow densities of 72 to 103 kg/m³ at six Rocky Mountain sites, so this rule is good to roughly ± 30 %: cold, dry powder gives more centimetres, wet snow fewer.

The probability is simply the share of members above a threshold τ: P(S > τ) = (1/N) Σ 1[S_i > τ], with N = 50 for ECMWF and N = 16 for GEFS. With τ equal to the 1991-2020 normal of the window, P is the chance of an above-normal period: 50 % means no signal, below 30 % a clear dry signal, above 70 % a clear snowy one. We also give the ratio R = mean(S) / normal and the snow share of precipitation φ = mean(S) / mean(P), which tells whether a wet spell falls as snow or rain at the height of a grid cell.

For days 16 to 21 GEFS has no snowfall field, so we build one: S = Σ P6h · CSNOW, the 6-hour precipitation counted only when the member's categorical snow flag is on. On the ground, NASA's MODIS reads snow with the normalised difference snow index, NDSI = (green - SWIR) / (green + SWIR), using band 6 at 1.6 µm (Hall et al. 2002; Riggs et al. 2019).

sections.h: Range by range: the next 15 days
p: Alps: a snowy first week, then a dry one. Across the Alpine cells above 1,000 m the ensemble mean is 19.1 mm of snow water for 24-30 November, against a normal of 17.8 mm, but only 9 mm for 1-8 December against 21.9 mm. Over the 15 days that adds up to 28.1 mm against 39.7 mm, and only 10 % of the members beat the normal.
Pyrenees: 19.1 mm against a normal of 18.3 mm, a near-normal fortnight with 46 % of members above normal, wetter in the west and centre than towards Andorra and Cerdanya.

Western US and Canada: 22.6 mm against 19.3 mm above 1,500 m, and 88 % of members above normal, the strongest snowy signal of the five ranges, carried by the Coast Mountains, the Sierra Nevada, Utah and Colorado.
Atlas: 0.9 mm against a normal of 4.4 mm, 4 % of members above normal. Andes: 2.9 mm against 5.4 mm, 12 %, as the southern spring dries out.

sections.h: Days 16 to 21: what NOAA GEFS adds
p: For 9 to 14 December the 16 complete GEFS members give these chances of above-normal snowfall: Atlas 25 %, Alps 12 %, Pyrenees 44 %, western US and Canada 38 %, Andes 31 %. Read them as a tilt, not a forecast. With 16 members each member is worth about 6 percentage points, and categorical snow flags tend to overcount wet snow near the melting level, so we only trust values far from 50 %.

sections.h: The circulation patterns that tilt the odds
p: The NAO (Hurrell 1995) is the pressure seesaw between Iceland and the Azores. A positive NAO steers Atlantic storms to northern Europe; a negative one sends them further south, towards Iberia, the Pyrenees and Morocco (Knippertz et al. 2003; López-Moreno and Vicente-Serrano 2007). NOAA's GEFS forecast brings the NAO from +0.97 on 26 November down to -0.29 by 4 December, with 60 % of the 31 member-days negative from day 8.

The Arctic Oscillation (Thompson and Wallace 1998) drops harder, to -1.34 on 2 December, with 77 % of member-days negative. A negative AO weakens the polar vortex and lets cold air spill south. The PNA (Wallace and Gutzler 1981) stays positive, +1.19 today and +0.23 on 9 December, a ridge over the West and trough over the East. In the south the AAO (Gong and Wang 1999) turns negative from 30 November, which usually pushes Pacific fronts closer to the Andes, though in late spring they bring less snow than in winter.

sections.h: What this outlook can and cannot tell you
p: Every number here is for a 0.25° cell, about 25 km across, whose mean height is often 500 to 1,000 m below the summits. The forecast smooths the peaks, so snowfall at a high resort is usually more than its cell says, and the snow line inside a cell can be very different from one valley to the next. That is why we compare ratios to the normal of the same cell rather than raw totals, and why the snow on the ground comes from NASA's 500 m MODIS maps, which see each slope, when clouds allow.

These are odds, not promises. A range with a 10 % chance of an above-normal fortnight can still get one big storm, and a 90 % signal can fizzle if one low-pressure system tracks 200 km off. For days 1 to 5, use a daily forecast; for avalanche conditions, use the official avalanche bulletins such as SLF. For water resources, snow on the ground matters more than snowfall, and remote sensing such as MODIS or the reconstructions of Durand et al. (2008) and Baba et al. (2018) is what turns it into snow water.

advice: Planning a trip in the next two weeks: the western US and Canada have the best odds (88 % above normal), then the Pyrenees.
In the Alps, the snow falls this week: the first days of December look calmer, so the best skiing is right after the storm, with a good base above about 1,000 m.
In the Atlas, do not count on fresh snow before mid-December; check again when the NAO turns clearly negative.
Odds beyond day 10 change from run to run: look at the trend over several days rather than one run.
